strengths: The Gaussian optimal-transport alignment followed by a residual Wasserstein distance is an interesting diagnostic of activation distributions. Computing signatures from forward activations offers a potentially useful way to compare vision architectures without retraining or calculating Jacobians.

The empirical survey is substantial: 33 architectures evaluated over all 50,000 ImageNet validation images, with additional CIFAR, random-input, and supervised/self-supervised comparisons. The visual signatures reveal recognizable architecture-family structure and differences between internal and post-residual activations.

The appendices provide useful checks beyond descriptive plots. Appendix C examines batch-size and training-seed sensitivity, while Appendix F compares ResNet20 with and without residual connections over five seeds, reporting accuracies of 91.74±0.28 and 90.77±0.24, respectively.
weaknesses: The central identification claim after Eq. (5) does not hold for the observed input-output mapping in general. The score depends only on marginal distributions. For example, let X be uniform on [0,1] and Y=1-|2X-1|. Y is also uniform, so T_aff is the identity and the affinity score equals 1, despite the transformation being non-affine. The positive-definite affine results establish a restricted sufficient condition, not the claimed general converse. The score can remain useful as a distributional diagnostic, but this distinction undermines its principal interpretation as a general measure of transformation non-linearity.

The practical estimator is not adequately connected to the theoretical quantity. Spatial averaging in Section 3.2 is lossy and can discard nonlinear behavior; Figure 2 demonstrates agreement for selected examples rather than general preservation. Likewise, matching shrunken covariance estimates does not necessarily match the actual covariances of the transported samples, so the population guarantees do not automatically survive shrinkage. Stability with dimensionality or batch size is useful evidence, but does not establish measurement accuracy.

The performance-prediction claim exceeds the evidence. Section 4.4 partitions architectures into families and selects the statistic maximizing absolute correlation on the same models used for evaluation. Figure 9 therefore establishes retrospective association, without held-out prediction or evidence that the relationship adds information beyond model scale and family. Appendix I includes relevant complexity baselines, but their correlations are already comparable: for traditional models, 0.755 for affinity versus 0.751 for depth; for efficient models, absolute correlations of 0.940 versus 0.932 for parameter count.

Comparative validation does not establish that the score measures non-linearity better than alternatives. Low correlation with CKA, sparsity, entropy, or fitted-linear-model R² in Section 4.2 establishes disagreement, not validity. Furthermore, Section 3.3's dismissal of Jacobian-based non-linearity measures because of ReLU non-differentiability is technically unconvincing: ReLU networks admit Jacobians almost everywhere. This leaves the closest methodological comparison insufficiently addressed.

Important numerical details remain ambiguous. The manuscript does not specify the empirical Wasserstein solver or treatment of zero-variance outputs, for which Eq. (5) has a zero denominator. Definition 3.1 also reverses the input-output argument order and places the activation after spatial reduction; averaging and activation generally do not commute. These affect reproducibility and interpretation, rather than being purely cosmetic issues. Together with the central validity gap and unvalidated predictive claim, they outweigh the worthwhile descriptive contribution and determine the weak-reject recommendation.
